probe.format_note: 1:1 square, 948 frames. The film is one 15.83 s loop (19 shots of exactly 25 frames = 0.833 s each) played twice: 15.83-31.6 s repeats 0-15.83 s frame for frame (scene-detect frame means match pairwise), and the last shot cuts straight back into the first, so the piece is built to loop. Stereo HE-AAC 44.1 kHz: dense, percussive electronic music with hits about every 0.2 s and stronger accents roughly every 0.6-0.8 s; every cut sits on the 0.833 s grid (every two beats at about 144 BPM, tempo inferred from the cut grid and a by-eye waveform, not measured).

rights_note: found by the owner on Pinterest with a style search (file «infographic motion design2.mp4»), given by the owner via Downloads/refrencee on 2026-11-03; origin not stated → plan mode ADAPT, never RECREATE

mode.alt_film_mode: EXPLAINER when the package walks through numbers or results step by step (one card per claim)
mode.why: third-party film of unknown origin: borrow the motion language and look only (hard cuts on the beat, flat KPI cards, counters, drawing charts, background colour flips), never its shots one by one, its brands, names, photos, copy or figures (owner note); a voiceover package defaults to REEL, and the reference itself is a fast KPI/marketing-results montage

method: ffprobe; ffmpeg contact sheets fps=2 at 480 px (6 sheets, all viewed; sheets 4-6 confirm the repeat); scene detect gt(scene,0.3): cuts at 0.833, 1.667, 2.5, 3.333, 4.167, 5.0, 5.833, 6.667, 7.5, 8.333, 9.167, 10.0, 10.833, 11.667, 12.5, 13.333, 14.167, 15.0, 15.833 s and the same grid again to 30.833 s, with matching frame means proving the loop; dense sheets fps=10 at 240 px over 0-15.84 s (4 sheets, all viewed; frame time = (sheet-1)*4 + index*0.1 s); audio waveform of 0-8 s (showwavespic) for the beat. Spans are frame-exact (25-frame grid); move durations read from the 0.1 s sheets, accurate to about ±0.1 s. Colours read by eye, not sampled.

visual_language: A fast, beat-cut KPI montage made of flat dashboard cards. Medium: crisp 2D UI built entirely in code — rounded stat cards, chart cards, chips, pills, avatars — plus two image shots (a photo with stickers, a live-action clip with a wireframe UI overlay). Typography: one clean geometric grotesque sans; numbers are the heroes (bold or medium, very large, tight tracking), labels are tiny caps overlines, body copy tiny and decorative; numbers use the European decimal comma. Rhythm: 19 shots in 15.83 s, every shot exactly 0.833 s (25 frames), every cut a hard cut on the beat (every two beats at about 144 BPM), and the film loops seamlessly. There are almost no entrances or exits: each shot opens already composed and lives through continuous inner motion — counters always counting up, bars filling, curves drawing, scrubber dots travelling, rings closing, a cursor selecting a bar — plus a slow drift or push of the whole composition. Only two shots have an arrival: the hero number slammed in from small with motion blur (r1-s2) and a chart card swinging flat from a 3D tilt (r1-s8). The background colour flips at almost every cut between four flat grounds (light grey, lavender, acid yellow, near-black), and the cards reuse the same four colours plus mint, orange and a success green, so the palette rotation itself is the rhythm. Signature moments: the full-width hero number with its pill badge, the 'with vs without' solid/dashed curves with a scrubber, the cursor turning a bar black, the progress ring, the split proportion bar with leader lines, stickers and wireframe UI laid over images, and the recurring card that returns inside a larger cluster.
look: Flat 2D, not 3D: solid flat backgrounds with no gradient, no texture and no ground plane; cards with rounded corners (about 2-3% of frame width), flat fills, no gradients except a soft glow on one yellow curve; shadows almost absent — at most a very soft, short drop shadow under stacked cards and faded ghost rows for depth; no depth of field; motion blur only on the hero-number slam; one brief CSS-3D tilt on a card entrance. Dense, editorial, slightly playful (emoji stickers, highlight strips), high contrast between near-black cards and pastel or acid grounds.
code_translation: Code-native. HTML/CSS/SVG in headless Chromium: flat rounded cards as divs; counters as per-frame interpolated numbers in Persian digits with the brand font (eased, ending exactly on the true value); bars and gauges as scaled rects with transform-origin at the baseline; curves as SVG paths revealed with stroke-dashoffset, a dashed comparison path via stroke-dasharray, a scrubber dot positioned along the path with getPointAtLength; progress ring as an SVG circle stroke; hero-number slam with scale + skew + directional blur (filter or frame blending) for about 5 frames; card tilt entrance with CSS perspective + rotateY/X; hard cuts are simple scene swaps on the beat grid; ghost rows as lower-opacity copies offset in y. Image slots (photo shots, avatars, product thumbnails) take owner assets unedited or code-drawn shapes. Nothing needs three.js.
continuity: Hard cut on every beat with no transition effects: continuity comes from rhythm, not from moves — the cut grid is fixed (two beats per shot) and every shot is the same length.
Background colour flip at every cut, rotating a small set of flat grounds (light, pastel, acid, near-black) so the cut itself reads as a beat and the film stays one system.
Never-still numbers: in every shot something is counting, filling or drawing from the first frame, so momentum carries across cuts even though nothing travels between them.
One card grammar everywhere (same corner radius, same type, same chip and pill shapes, same four colours), so very different data still reads as one dashboard.
A component seen alone returns later inside a larger cluster (recomposition instead of a camera zoom), and a whole-system overview shot gathers earlier screens small together.
Cards bleed off the frame edges and overlap each other with small offsets and chips pinned over their corners, implying a larger canvas beyond the frame.
Inner guides of attention: a cursor selecting a bar, a scrubber dot riding a curve, a chip sliding along a connector — each points the eye at the value that matters in that beat.
Seamless loop: the last shot cuts straight back to the first on the beat.
risks: Third-party film of unknown origin: ADAPT only. Never copy its brand names, product names, people, photos, footage, copy, placeholder text, figures or the shot order one by one.

Shots are 0.833 s each: far too short to read Persian. Readability ranks above the reference: keep hard cuts on a beat grid and the colour flips, but lengthen each card beat to the voice phrase it shows (and to the hold time in data-viz.md), e.g. two or three beats of our own track per card; use the 0.833 s pace only for purely visual punctuation.

Counters run in every shot: in our film every counter must end exactly on the package's sourced value (data-viz.md), use Persian digits and the Persian decimal separator, and never count a figure the package does not contain.
Source is 1:1 square: a 9:16 film rebuilds each composition vertically (cards stacked, hero number scaled to the width inside the safe zone); a 16:9 film widens the clusters.

Charts and bars in the reference read left → right (scrubber left → right, bars split from the left, cursor moving right): direction for Persian follows references/rtl-grammar.md; time axes and curves may keep a direction only where the rtl grammar allows it.

Two shots are a real photo and live footage (r1-s9, r1-s17) and several cards hold portraits and product photos: these are not code-buildable; use the overlay devices only over owner assets or code-drawn subjects, never third-party faces or stock people.

Reference colours (light grey, lavender, acid yellow, near-black, mint, orange, green) map onto brand colour roles (light background, primary/secondary, accent, dark background, success); never used as literal hex values. Colours were read by eye, not sampled.

The reference has its own music with cuts every two beats; our film's cuts follow the voiceover first, and L6 places accents on our cuts rather than reusing their music. Tempo was inferred, not measured.
Emoji stickers and the playful tone: use only where the package's tone and the brand allow; the brand's banned colours and owner decisions still win.
